summary: Specifies the process for selecting, confirming and recalling the members of the IAB and IESG, including how the nominating and recall committees operate. It replaces RFC 2027 and was replaced by RFC 2727.

eli5.summary: It is the rulebook for how the leaders of the Internet's standards groups are chosen and, if needed, removed.

questions: how are iab and iesg members selected
how can ietf leaders be recalled
subtitle: The rulebook for electing Internet standards leaders.

tldr.problem: The IETF needed a formal, written process for selecting and removing the leaders of the IAB and IESG, which had previously been passed down only by tradition.
tldr.mechanism: The process uses a nominating committee drawn from the community, which proposes candidates to a confirming body. Members serve staggered two-year terms with half the positions reviewed each year.
tldr.outcome: This specification was superseded by RFC 2727, which refined the process further.

facts.label: Committee composition
facts.value: Chair plus 10 voting members plus 3 liaisons

today: RFC 2282 was superseded by RFC 2727, which replaced it in December 1999. Consult RFC 2727 for the current process.

sections.title: Selecting and Confirming Leaders
sections.content:
RFC 2282 specifies the process for selecting the members of the IAB (Internet Architecture Board) and IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group), the leadership bodies of the IETF. Before this document, the process existed only as oral tradition passed between committees. This document organizes the rules that the 1996 nominating committee discovered through experience.

The process covers selection (which volunteers to nominate), confirmation (approval by the appropriate body), and recall (removal if warranted). The process assumes IETF meetings occur at least once a year in the North American spring.
sections.eli5: This is the official rulebook for how to pick and remove the people who lead the Internet's standards groups.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The process distinguishes between nominees (people being considered) and candidates (nominees selected by the committee to go to the confirming body). A confirmed candidate is approved by the confirming body and becomes a member.

The process has several important constraints. About half of the IESG and IAB positions are reviewed each year to ensure regular turnover. Confirmed members serve a minimum two-year term. All deliberations about specific people are confidential to protect privacy during the selection process.

The process uses an advise and consent model: the nominating committee advises the confirming body of candidates, and the confirming body consents by majority vote. If a candidate is rejected, the committee must reconvene to find an alternative.
sections.eli5: The process carefully separates the job of picking candidates (the nominating committee) from the job of approving them (the IAB or the Internet Society board). This keeps any one group from having too much power.

sections.title: Nominating Committee Structure and Process
sections.content:
The nominating committee comprises at least a non-voting Chair (appointed by the Internet Society President), 10 voting members drawn randomly from the IETF community, and 3 non-voting liaisons. A quorum for voting is at least 7 voting members.

To volunteer, a community member must have attended at least 2 of the last 3 IETF meetings. However, sitting members of the IESG, IAB, or Internet Society Board may not volunteer.

The Chair establishes and publicizes milestones for the selection process, ensures a fair and unbiased random selection method, and has discretion to handle exceptional circumstances. The process requires consulting a broad base of the community when selecting candidates, though all discussions remain confidential.

The nominating committee also has the option to establish a recall process for its own members by a 3/4 majority vote.
sections.eli5: The committee is chosen randomly from volunteers who have been active in IETF meetings. The Chair runs the process, sets deadlines, and keeps discussions secret until candidates are approved.

sections.title: Removing a Member
sections.content:
Any IETF community member may request the recall of a sitting IAB or IESG member at any time, by written request with justification to the Internet Society President. The President appoints a Recall Committee Chair but explicitly does not evaluate the request; that is the community's responsibility.

The recall committee is formed by the same rules as the nominating committee, except the person being recalled and the person requesting the recall cannot serve on it. The committee operates by the same rules as the nominating committee but with no confirmation process.

The committee investigates the circumstances, giving the member a chance to provide a written statement and consulting third parties. A 3/4 majority vote is required to recall the member. If recalled, the position is filled by the mid-term vacancy rules, which require the nominating committee to fill it within one month.
sections.eli5: If the Internet community has concerns about a leader, anyone can ask for a formal investigation. A special committee looks into it, the member gets to explain, and if 3 out of 4 committee members agree, the person is removed.

sections.title: Confidentiality and Responsibility
sections.content:
The process involves investigation into the qualifications and activities of candidates, which may reveal confidential or private information. Everyone who participates—committee members, consulted experts, those providing information—bears responsibility for maintaining strict confidentiality of any information not explicitly identified for public release.

This protects candidates from reputational harm, ensures candid feedback during the selection process, and respects the privacy of people being considered for leadership roles.
sections.eli5: Because the process involves asking people questions about candidates, all participants promise to keep that information secret to protect people's privacy.
